items.stem: A company connects its data center to one VPC with two Site-to-Site VPN connections to a virtual private gateway. The connections use static routing. Nightly transfers now need several times the bandwidth of one VPN tunnel, and the design must be scalable as the transfers grow. The company does not want to use AWS Direct Connect yet. The customer gateway devices support BGP. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)
keywords: several times the bandwidth of one VPN tunnel
The customer gateway devices support BGP

options.text: Attach the VPN connections to a transit gateway instead of the virtual private gateway, and turn on equal-cost multi-path (ECMP) routing support on it.
options.why: On a virtual private gateway [ECMP is not supported for Site-to-Site VPN connections](../facts/site-to-site-vpn.md#site-to-site-vpn-ecmp-not-on-vgw-supported-on-tgw); for higher throughput the VPN FAQ says to [use AWS Transit Gateway](../facts/site-to-site-vpn.md#site-to-site-vpn-faq-tgw-for-higher-throughput).

options.text: Add three more Site-to-Site VPN connections to the existing virtual private gateway, and spread the data center prefixes across all of the tunnels.
options.why: On a virtual private gateway [ECMP is not supported for Site-to-Site VPN connections](../facts/site-to-site-vpn.md#site-to-site-vpn-ecmp-not-on-vgw-supported-on-tgw), so the gateway uses one tunnel and more connections add no bandwidth.

options.text: Turn on acceleration for the existing VPN connections, so that the tunnels use the AWS global network and carry more traffic each night.
options.why: [You cannot turn on or turn off acceleration](../facts/site-to-site-vpn.md#site-to-site-vpn-accelerated-cannot-toggle-on-existing) on an existing connection, and virtual private gateways [do not support accelerated VPN connections](../facts/site-to-site-vpn.md#site-to-site-vpn-accelerated-transit-gateway-only).
options.misconception: acceleration can be turned on for an existing VPN connection on a virtual private gateway

options.text: Use dynamic routing with BGP for the VPN connections, and advertise the data center prefixes from the customer gateway devices on every tunnel.
options.why: For ECMP the VPN connections [must be configured for dynamic routing](../facts/site-to-site-vpn.md#site-to-site-vpn-ecmp-needs-dynamic-routing-not-static), because [ECMP is not supported using static routing](../facts/site-to-site-vpn.md#site-to-site-vpn-tgw-vpn-ecmp-requires-dynamic-routing-whitepaper).

options.text: Replace the virtual private gateway with software VPN appliances on Amazon EC2 instances, and split the tunnels across the instances with custom routing scripts.
options.why: Appliances can spread the load, but [you must manage the software appliance](../facts/site-to-site-vpn.md#site-to-site-vpn-software-vpn-ec2-you-manage-appliance-single-point-of-failure) and its scripts, which is more work than a transit gateway.

items.explanation: The deciding phrase is several times the bandwidth of one tunnel. A transit gateway spreads traffic across many tunnels with ECMP, and the connections [must be configured for dynamic routing](../facts/site-to-site-vpn.md#site-to-site-vpn-ecmp-needs-dynamic-routing-not-static). On a virtual private gateway, [ECMP is not supported for Site-to-Site VPN connections](../facts/site-to-site-vpn.md#site-to-site-vpn-ecmp-not-on-vgw-supported-on-tgw).
items.takeaway: More VPN bandwidth than one tunnel comes from a transit gateway with ECMP and BGP, not from more connections on a virtual private gateway.
items.twin: If the stem said "The customer gateway devices do not support BGP" instead: new devices come first, because [ECMP is not supported using static routing](../facts/site-to-site-vpn.md#site-to-site-vpn-tgw-vpn-ecmp-requires-dynamic-routing-whitepaper).
items.say: I'd move the VPNs to a transit gateway and run BGP, so ECMP spreads the traffic over all the tunnels.

solvers.stem_only: Move the VPN connections from the virtual private gateway to a transit gateway with ECMP support turned on, and switch the connections to dynamic (BGP) routing so the same prefixes are advertised on all tunnels; ECMP then spreads traffic across tunnels and scales by adding connections.

items.stem: A company runs a mission-critical application in AWS that reads order data from its on-premises data center every minute. The data center connects to AWS through one AWS Direct Connect dedicated connection at one Direct Connect location. The connectivity must survive the failure of a device, a connection, or a whole Direct Connect location. Which design will make the connectivity the MOST resilient?

options.text: Add three dedicated connections at the current location, and combine all four connections in a link aggregation group (LAG) for the traffic.
options.why: A LAG ends at one location, and it [will not protect against a single device failure](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-lag-not-more-resilient-against-device-failure) there or against the loss of that location.

options.text: Keep the current dedicated connection, and add a Site-to-Site VPN connection over the internet as the backup path for the traffic.
options.why: A VPN backup avoids the location, but [performance over the internet is best effort](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-vs-vpn-internet-vpn-best-effort-low-cost-widely-available), so it ranks below a second Direct Connect location.

options.text: Add a second dedicated connection at the current location, and make sure that it ends on a different AWS device from the first one.
options.why: Connections that [terminate on separate devices in one location](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-resiliency-dev-test-one-location-no-location-failure-protection) give no protection when that whole location fails.
options.misconception: separate devices at one Direct Connect location also protect against the loss of that location

options.text: Add connections at a second Direct Connect location, so that each of the two locations has two connections that end on separate devices.
options.why: Connections on [separate devices in more than one location](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-resiliency-maximum-separate-devices-more-than-one-location) give [resiliency against device, connectivity, and complete location failures](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-resiliency-maximum-separate-devices-more-than-one-location).

items.explanation: The deciding phrase is the failure of a whole Direct Connect location. AWS recommends [making connections at multiple AWS Direct Connect locations](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-faq-high-availability-multiple-locations), and the maximum resiliency model can reach [an SLA of 99.99%](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-resiliency-maximum-sla-99-99) when you meet the SLA requirements.
items.takeaway: The most resilient Direct Connect design uses two locations and separate devices, not a LAG at one location.
items.twin: If the stem said "a development workload that can stop when a location fails" instead: two connections at one location, because that model uses connections that [terminate on separate devices in one location](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-resiliency-dev-test-one-location-no-location-failure-protection).
items.say: For critical traffic I'd put Direct Connect connections on separate devices in two locations.

solvers.stem_only: Maximum resiliency model: two Direct Connect locations, each with two connections terminating on separate devices, so a device, connection or whole location can fail.

items.stem: A company has one AWS Direct Connect dedicated connection at a location in the United States. A private virtual interface on the connection is attached to the virtual private gateway of a VPC in us-east-1. The company adds a VPC in eu-west-1, a second Region, and that VPC must reach the data center privately over the same connection. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create a second private virtual interface on the connection, and attach it directly to the virtual private gateway of the VPC in eu-west-1.
options.why: Attached directly, a private virtual interface [reaches a VPC in the associated Region only](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-private-vif-without-dxgw-reaches-associated-region-only), and this connection is in the United States.
options.misconception: a private virtual interface attached directly to a virtual private gateway reaches a VPC in any Region

options.text: Create a public virtual interface on the connection, and use it to reach the private IP addresses of the VPC in eu-west-1.
options.why: A public virtual interface [enables access to public services](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-faq-vif-public-vs-private) such as Amazon S3; a private virtual interface [enables access to your VPC](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-faq-vif-public-vs-private).
options.misconception: a public virtual interface reaches the private IP addresses of a VPC

options.text: Create a Direct Connect gateway, attach a new private virtual interface to it, and associate the virtual private gateways of both VPCs with it.
options.why: Through a Direct Connect gateway, one private virtual interface reaches virtual private gateways [across any account and AWS Region](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-private-vif-single-vpc-or-dxgw-many-regions), so both VPCs share the connection.

options.text: Create a transit gateway in each Region, attach each VPC to the transit gateway in its Region, and connect both through a transit virtual interface.
options.why: A transit virtual interface is [attached to an AWS Direct Connect gateway](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-transit-vif-attaches-only-to-dxgw) and can reach both, but two transit gateways add attachments and route tables to run.

items.explanation: The deciding phrases are a second Region and the same connection. A Direct Connect gateway is [a globally available resource](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-dxgw-global-resource-any-region-not-china), and with it you reach [any AWS Region](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-faq-dxgw-any-region-from-any-location) from a Direct Connect location. Associating both virtual private gateways with it is the smallest change.
items.takeaway: One Direct Connect connection reaches VPCs in several Regions through a Direct Connect gateway.
items.twin: If the stem said "a second VPC in us-east-1" instead: a second private virtual interface to that VPC also works, because the VPC has [a virtual private gateway in the same Region](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-private-vif-without-dxgw-reaches-associated-region-only).
items.say: I'd add a Direct Connect gateway, because one private virtual interface on it reaches VPCs in any Region.

steps: I read the last sentence first: it asks for the solution with the LEAST operational overhead.
I mark the constraints: one existing connection in the United States, a new VPC in eu-west-1, private access, and the same connection.
Before I look at the options, I predict a Direct Connect gateway, because it is a global resource that lets one private virtual interface reach VPCs in other Regions.

I remove the public virtual interface, because it reaches public services, not the private addresses of a VPC. I remove the direct attachment in eu-west-1, because a private virtual interface without a gateway reaches the associated Region only.

Between the Direct Connect gateway and the two transit gateways the difference is what the team must run; the stem asks for the LEAST operational overhead, so the transit gateways add work without a feature that the stem needs.
Check: the Direct Connect gateway uses the same connection, stays private, and reaches both Regions. Time: 90 seconds.

solvers.stem_only: Create a Direct Connect gateway, put a private virtual interface on it, and associate the virtual private gateways of both VPCs (any Region) with the Direct Connect gateway.

items.stem: A company has employees who work from home on laptops. The employees must reach internal applications that run on Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets of a VPC in one AWS Region. They must sign in with the company's existing SAML 2.0 identity provider. The company wants a fully managed remote access solution. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create a Site-to-Site VPN connection from each laptop to a virtual private gateway, with one customer gateway for each employee.
options.why: Site-to-Site VPN is for connecting [an entire on-premises network](../facts/site-to-site-vpn.md#site-to-site-vpn-decision-guide-connect-entire-network-to-vpcs) to VPCs, not single laptops of remote employees.

options.text: Create an AWS Client VPN endpoint that uses federated authentication with the SAML 2.0 identity provider, and give users the AWS provided client.
options.why: [AWS Client VPN supports identity federation with Security Assertion Markup Language 2.0 (SAML 2.0)](../facts/client-vpn.md#client-vpn-saml-federated-authentication-single-idp), and users connect with the AWS provided client.

options.text: Run an OpenVPN server on an Amazon EC2 instance, connect it to the identity provider, and patch and scale the instance as users grow.
options.why: It works, but the team patches and scales the instance itself; Client VPN is [an AWS managed high availability and scalability service](../facts/client-vpn.md#client-vpn-whitepaper-managed-secure-software-remote-access).

options.text: Order an AWS Direct Connect hosted connection for each home office, and attach a private virtual interface to the VPC for each one.
options.why: Direct Connect gives [dedicated, private network connections](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-faq-bypasses-internet-dedicated-private) between a network and AWS, so a circuit to each home solves a problem the employees do not have.
options.misconception: Direct Connect is a way to connect individual remote users

items.explanation: The deciding phrases are employees on laptops and the SAML 2.0 identity provider. AWS says to consider Client VPN to [securely connect remote users to your VPCs](../facts/client-vpn.md#client-vpn-vs-site-to-site-decision-guide-remote-users), and Client VPN is [a managed client-based VPN service](../facts/client-vpn.md#client-vpn-definition-managed-client-based-vpn-openvpn).
items.takeaway: People on laptops use Client VPN; whole networks use Site-to-Site VPN.
items.twin: If the stem said "a branch office network" instead: a Site-to-Site VPN connection, because it can connect [an entire on-premises network](../facts/site-to-site-vpn.md#site-to-site-vpn-decision-guide-connect-entire-network-to-vpcs) to VPCs.
items.say: For people on laptops I'd use Client VPN with SAML sign-in, not a Site-to-Site VPN.

solvers.stem_only: AWS Client VPN endpoint associated with the VPC subnets, using SAML 2.0 federated authentication with the existing IdP; users connect with the AWS provided client.

items.stem: A company uses a 10 Gbps AWS Direct Connect connection as the primary path from its data center to a virtual private gateway. A Site-to-Site VPN connection to the same virtual private gateway is the backup path for this mission-critical traffic. However, in a failover test, the VPN cannot carry the load. The company needs a highly available design in which the backup path carries the full load when the primary connection fails. Which solution will provide the HIGHEST availability?
keywords: the VPN cannot carry the load

options.text: Use AS path prepending on the Direct Connect routes, so that the VPN connection carries part of the traffic at all times.
options.why: The Direct Connect path wins [regardless of AS path prepending](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-vpn-same-vpc-failover-only-dx-path-preferred), so the VPN carries traffic only after a failure.

options.text: Add three more Site-to-Site VPN connections to the same virtual private gateway, so that the backup tunnels can share the full load.
options.why: On a virtual private gateway [ECMP is not supported for Site-to-Site VPN connections](../facts/site-to-site-vpn.md#site-to-site-vpn-ecmp-not-on-vgw-supported-on-tgw), so one tunnel of [up to 1.25 Gbps](../facts/site-to-site-vpn.md#site-to-site-vpn-limit-bandwidth-standard-tunnel) carries the backup, far below the 10 Gbps load.

options.text: Order a second 10 Gbps Direct Connect connection at a second Direct Connect location, and use it as the backup path for the traffic.
options.why: AWS recommends [making connections at multiple AWS Direct Connect locations](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-faq-high-availability-multiple-locations), so the second connection carries the full load even when the first location fails.

options.text: Order a second 10 Gbps connection at the same Direct Connect location, and add both connections to one link aggregation group (LAG).
options.why: It carries the load after one link fails, but a LAG [will not protect against a single device failure](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-lag-not-more-resilient-against-device-failure) where it ends.

items.explanation: The deciding phrase is the full load of a 10 Gbps connection. A VPN on a virtual private gateway gives [up to 1.25 Gbps throughput per VPN tunnel](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-backup-vpn-bandwidth-limit-not-above-1-gbps), and teams that ignore this [overestimate their backup capabilities](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-wa-anti-pattern-overestimating-vpn-backup-bandwidth). A second Direct Connect connection at another location carries the same load.
items.takeaway: Back up a fast Direct Connect connection with another Direct Connect connection at a second location.
items.twin: If the stem said "a non-critical workload on a 1 Gbps connection" instead: a VPN backup is a fair choice, because one tunnel gives [up to 1.25 Gbps throughput per VPN tunnel](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-backup-vpn-bandwidth-limit-not-above-1-gbps).
items.say: A VPN can't back up a 10 gig Direct Connect line, so I'd add a second connection at another location.

solvers.stem_only: Replace the VPN backup with a second Direct Connect connection of the same capacity at a different Direct Connect location, so the backup carries the full load and no single location is a point of failure.

items.stem: A company has a Site-to-Site VPN connection between its data center and a virtual private gateway. The customer gateway device has only one of the two tunnels configured, and it uses static routing. During an AWS tunnel endpoint update, connectivity to the VPC stopped for several minutes. The company needs the VPN to be highly available, with minimal downtime during future updates. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: only one of the two tunnels configured

options.text: Attach a second virtual private gateway to the VPC, and create a second VPN connection with one tunnel that ends on the new gateway.
options.why: You can attach [one virtual private gateway to a VPC](../facts/site-to-site-vpn.md#site-to-site-vpn-vgw-attaches-to-single-vpc) at a time, so a second gateway cannot be attached.
options.misconception: a VPC can have two virtual private gateways at the same time

options.text: Turn on tunnel endpoint lifecycle control for the connection, and schedule each AWS update for a time when the single tunnel is not busy.
options.why: Lifecycle control gives [control over the schedule of endpoint replacements](../facts/site-to-site-vpn.md#site-to-site-vpn-elc-control-schedule-of-endpoint-replacements), but the single tunnel still goes down during each replacement.

options.text: Configure the second tunnel of the existing VPN connection on the customer gateway device, so that traffic can move to it during an update.
options.why: AWS says to [configure both tunnels for redundancy](../facts/site-to-site-vpn.md#site-to-site-vpn-two-tunnels-unique-public-ip-configure-both); when one tunnel is down, traffic is [automatically routed to the available tunnel](../facts/site-to-site-vpn.md#site-to-site-vpn-two-tunnels-unique-public-ip-configure-both).

options.text: Create a second VPN connection to the same virtual private gateway from a new customer gateway device, and configure one tunnel on each device.
options.why: It adds redundancy, but a new device and a second connection are more work than configuring the tunnel that the connection already has.

items.explanation: The deciding fact is the single configured tunnel. AWS [applies tunnel endpoint updates to one tunnel](../facts/site-to-site-vpn.md#site-to-site-vpn-endpoint-update-one-tunnel-at-a-time) at a time, so a second tunnel keeps the connection up. During a replacement, [connectivity over the tunnel might be interrupted](../facts/site-to-site-vpn.md#site-to-site-vpn-endpoint-replacement-interrupts-tunnel), which is what the company saw.
items.takeaway: Configure both tunnels of every Site-to-Site VPN connection, so that AWS updates do not stop the traffic.
items.twin: If the stem said "both tunnels are configured, but failover between them is slow" instead: dynamic routing with BGP, because AWS says to [use BGP-capable devices, when available](../facts/site-to-site-vpn.md#site-to-site-vpn-bgp-recommended-liveness-failover).
items.say: AWS updates one tunnel at a time, so I'd configure the second tunnel on the device.

solvers.stem_only: Configure the second tunnel of the existing VPN connection on the customer gateway device; AWS updates one tunnel at a time, so traffic fails over to the other tunnel.

verification.note: kept as a verified reserve; q012 ships instead to test Client VPN design (finding exam-03)

items.stem: A company must connect its on-premises data center to a VPC in one AWS Region. All traffic between the data center and the VPC must be encrypted in transit. The connection must be ready as soon as possible, within one week, and the traffic is low. The company has a router in the data center that supports IPsec. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: as soon as possible, within one week

options.text: Create a Site-to-Site VPN connection over the internet from the data center router to a virtual private gateway that is attached to the VPC.
options.why: A Site-to-Site VPN [can be configured in minutes](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-faq-vpn-ipsec-over-internet-quick-low-bandwidth) and suits [low to modest bandwidth requirements](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-faq-vpn-ipsec-over-internet-quick-low-bandwidth), so it meets the deadline with IPsec encryption.

options.text: Order a new AWS Direct Connect dedicated connection, and create a Site-to-Site VPN connection over it from the data center router to the VPC.
options.why: A new dedicated connection can take [from several weeks to a few months](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-vs-vpn-time-dedicated-weeks-to-months) to install, so it misses the one-week deadline.

options.text: Launch a software VPN appliance on an Amazon EC2 instance in the VPC, and connect it to the data center router with IPsec over the internet.
options.why: It works, but [you must manage the software appliance](../facts/site-to-site-vpn.md#site-to-site-vpn-software-vpn-ec2-you-manage-appliance-single-point-of-failure), including its patches, which is more work than a Site-to-Site VPN connection.

options.text: Order a new AWS Direct Connect dedicated connection, and launch a software VPN appliance on an Amazon EC2 instance that ends IPsec over the connection.
options.why: The new dedicated connection takes [from several weeks to a few months](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-vs-vpn-time-dedicated-weeks-to-months), so the design fails the deadline before the appliance adds its own work.

items.explanation: The deciding phrases are the one-week deadline and the low traffic. A Site-to-Site VPN gives [Internet Protocol security (IPsec) VPN connections](../facts/site-to-site-vpn.md#site-to-site-vpn-definition-ipsec-vpc-to-on-premises) between the data center and the VPC, and it [can be configured in minutes](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-faq-vpn-ipsec-over-internet-quick-low-bandwidth). A new Direct Connect dedicated connection takes [from several weeks to a few months](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-vs-vpn-time-dedicated-weeks-to-months), with or without a VPN on top.
items.takeaway: A deadline of days and low traffic point to a Site-to-Site VPN, not a new Direct Connect port.
items.twin: If the stem said "The company needs consistent network performance for large, steady transfers, and the connection can be ready in four months" instead: a VPN over Direct Connect, for [more consistent performance than the internet can provide](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-decision-guide-more-consistent-performance-than-internet).
items.say: With a one-week deadline I'd start with a Site-to-Site VPN, because a new Direct Connect port takes weeks.

solvers.stem_only: AWS Site-to-Site VPN over the internet from the existing IPsec router (customer gateway) to a virtual private gateway on the VPC; quick to set up, encrypted, fine for low traffic.

items.stem: A company sends traffic from its data center to a VPC over a private line: an AWS Direct Connect connection with a transit virtual interface that reaches the VPC through a Direct Connect gateway and a transit gateway. Dozens of applications send data over this connection. A new security rule says that all traffic on this connection must be encrypted in transit. The connection is a 1 Gbps hosted connection from a Direct Connect Partner. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Turn on MACsec for the Direct Connect connection, and configure the matching MACsec keys on the company router at the Direct Connect location.
options.why: MACsec is [not supported on 1 Gbps dedicated connections](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-macsec-not-on-1gbps-or-hosted) or on [any hosted connections](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-macsec-not-on-1gbps-or-hosted), so it cannot run on this connection.
options.misconception: MACsec works on every Direct Connect connection, hosted ones included

options.text: Create a Site-to-Site VPN on the transit gateway that runs IPsec over the Direct Connect connection, and route VPC traffic through its tunnels.
options.why: A private IP VPN can [deploy IPsec VPN over Direct Connect](../facts/site-to-site-vpn.md#site-to-site-vpn-private-ip-vpn-ipsec-over-dx-no-public-ip) on the existing transit virtual interface, so one network change encrypts all the traffic without changes in the applications.

options.text: Keep the current design, because traffic on a Direct Connect connection stays off the internet and is encrypted on the private line.
options.why: Direct Connect [does not encrypt your traffic](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-not-encrypted-by-default-use-service-encryption) in transit by default, so the private line alone breaks the new security rule.

options.text: Turn on TLS encryption in every application that sends data between the data center and the VPC, and keep the virtual interface unchanged.
options.why: It works, because you can [use the transit encryption options for that service](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-not-encrypted-by-default-use-service-encryption), but changing dozens of applications is more work than one VPN.

items.explanation: The deciding phrase is the 1 Gbps hosted connection. Direct Connect [does not encrypt your traffic](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-not-encrypted-by-default-use-service-encryption) by default, so you [establish a VPN over Direct Connect](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-encrypt-private-connection-vpn-over-dx-or-macsec) or use MACsec. MACsec does not run on [any hosted connections](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-macsec-not-on-1gbps-or-hosted), which leaves the IPsec VPN. A transit virtual interface works on a [dedicated or hosted connection of any speed](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-vif-transit-access-transit-gateways-any-speed), so the VPN uses the existing one.
items.takeaway: Direct Connect is private but not encrypted; on a hosted connection, add an IPsec VPN instead of MACsec.
items.twin: If the stem said "The connection is a 10 Gbps dedicated connection, the router and location support MACsec, and the encryption must not reduce the MTU" instead: MACsec, because [MACsec does not have the same MTU](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-vpn-over-dx-adds-encryption-reduces-mtu) considerations.
items.say: Direct Connect isn't encrypted by default, and MACsec doesn't run on hosted connections, so I'd run an IPsec VPN over it.

solvers.stem_only: MACsec is not an option because it is offered only on dedicated connections at higher speeds, not on a 1 Gbps hosted connection. Adding TLS to dozens of applications is high overhead. Run an IPsec Site-to-Site VPN over the Direct Connect connection (private IP VPN terminating on the transit gateway via the transit virtual interface) and route VPC traffic through its tunnels: one central change encrypts all traffic.

items.stem: A company runs an analytics workload in a VPC. The company needs a private line from its data center to the VPC that does not use the internet. A capacity of 200 Mbps is sufficient for the next three years. The company has no network equipment in a Direct Connect location and does not want to place any there. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?
keywords: no network equipment in a Direct Connect location

options.text: Request a 200 Mbps dedicated connection in the Direct Connect console, and order a cross-connect at the Direct Connect location.
options.why: A dedicated connection has a port speed of [1 Gbps, 10 Gbps, 100 Gbps, and 400 Gbps](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-limit-dedicated-port-speeds), so 200 Mbps is not a dedicated speed.
options.misconception: a dedicated connection can be ordered at any speed

options.text: Request a 10 Gbps dedicated connection, and work with a partner to extend the data center network to the Direct Connect location.
options.why: It works, but port hours are charged even when [no data is passing through the port](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-port-hours-charged-even-when-no-data), so the larger port costs more for capacity that the company does not use.

options.text: Create a Site-to-Site VPN connection over the internet to a virtual private gateway, and size the customer gateway device for 200 Mbps.
options.why: It costs less, but the stem rules out the internet, and a Site-to-Site VPN runs [over the public internet](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-faq-vpn-ipsec-over-internet-quick-low-bandwidth).

options.text: Ask an AWS Direct Connect Partner for a 200 Mbps hosted connection, and create a private virtual interface on it to the VPC.
options.why: A partner [provisions on behalf of a customer](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-hosted-connection-provisioned-by-partner) a hosted connection, so the company pays for the capacity it needs and places no equipment.

items.explanation: The deciding phrases are 200 Mbps and no equipment in a Direct Connect location. Partners [can help you extend your preexisting data center](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-partners-extend-network-to-location) to a Direct Connect location. A partner [provisions on behalf of a customer](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-hosted-connection-provisioned-by-partner) a hosted connection of the size the company orders, so the company pays for no unused port capacity.
items.takeaway: For a small capacity and no equipment at a location, ask a partner for a hosted connection.
items.twin: If the stem said "The connection can use the internet" instead: a Site-to-Site VPN, because it has [low cost and is widely available](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-vs-vpn-internet-vpn-best-effort-low-cost-widely-available).
items.say: For 200 megabits and no gear at a location, I'd ask a partner for a hosted connection.

solvers.stem_only: A 200 Mbps hosted connection ordered through a Direct Connect Partner, with a private virtual interface to the VPC; no equipment at the Direct Connect location and no oversized dedicated port.

items.stem: A company has an AWS Client VPN endpoint that is associated with a subnet of a VPC, and remote users reach resources in that VPC. The VPC reaches an on-premises network, 172.16.0.0/16, through a Site-to-Site VPN connection, and its route tables and security groups already allow traffic from the client CIDR range. Users must also reach the on-premises network through Client VPN. The company wants to restrict the tunnel to traffic for the VPC and the on-premises network. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)
keywords: must also reach the on-premises network
restrict the tunnel to traffic for the VPC and the on-premises network

options.text: Change the client CIDR range of the endpoint to 172.16.0.0/22, so that clients get addresses inside the on-premises network range.
options.why: [The client CIDR range cannot be changed](../facts/client-vpn.md#client-vpn-client-cidr-cannot-change-after-creation) after you create the endpoint, and clients need a route, not on-premises addresses.
options.misconception: the client CIDR range of a Client VPN endpoint can be changed later

options.text: Add a route to 172.16.0.0/16 through the associated subnet in the endpoint route table, and add an authorization rule for 172.16.0.0/16.
options.why: To reach another network, you [add a route to the specific network](../facts/client-vpn.md#client-vpn-other-networks-need-route-and-authorization-rule) in the endpoint route table and [add authorization rule enabling access](../facts/client-vpn.md#client-vpn-other-networks-need-route-and-authorization-rule) to it.

options.text: Add an authorization rule that denies access to 0.0.0.0/0, so that internet traffic from the clients cannot use the tunnel.
options.why: [The default behavior is to deny access](../facts/client-vpn.md#client-vpn-authorization-rules-default-deny-no-restrict-rules), and you [cannot add an authorization rule to restrict access](../facts/client-vpn.md#client-vpn-authorization-rules-default-deny-no-restrict-rules) to a network.
options.misconception: a Client VPN authorization rule can deny access to a network

options.text: Create a new Client VPN endpoint with split-tunnel turned on, copy the routes and rules to it, and move every user to the new endpoint.
options.why: It works, because split-tunnel can be turned on [on a new or existing Client VPN endpoint](../facts/client-vpn.md#client-vpn-split-tunnel-disabled-by-default-at-creation), but a new endpoint and new user profiles are more work.

options.text: Turn on split-tunnel on the existing endpoint, so that only traffic that matches a route in the endpoint route table uses the tunnel.
options.why: By default [all traffic from clients is routed](../facts/client-vpn.md#client-vpn-split-tunnel-default-off-all-traffic-through-tunnel) over the tunnel; with split-tunnel on, [only traffic with a destination to the network](../facts/client-vpn.md#client-vpn-split-tunnel-default-off-all-traffic-through-tunnel) of a route uses it.

items.explanation: Two gaps exist. A network outside the VPC needs a route and an authorization rule on the endpoint. With split-tunnel on, [only traffic with a destination to the network](../facts/client-vpn.md#client-vpn-split-tunnel-default-off-all-traffic-through-tunnel) of a route goes over the tunnel, so internet traffic stays on the local network.
items.takeaway: Client VPN reaches another network through a route plus an authorization rule; split-tunnel limits what uses the tunnel.
items.twin: If the stem said "all user traffic, including internet traffic, must go through the tunnel" instead: keep split-tunnel off, because then [all traffic from clients is routed](../facts/client-vpn.md#client-vpn-split-tunnel-default-off-all-traffic-through-tunnel) through it.
items.say: I'd add a route and an authorization rule for the on-premises network, and turn on split-tunnel.

solvers.stem_only: On the existing endpoint: add a route for 172.16.0.0/16 through the associated subnet plus an authorization rule for it, and turn on split-tunnel (modifiable in place) so only routed VPC and on-premises traffic uses the tunnel.

items.stem: A company must connect its on-premises data center to a VPC in one AWS Region. All traffic between the data center and the VPC must be encrypted in transit. The company needs consistent network performance for large, steady transfers, and the connection can be ready in four months. The company has a router in the data center that supports IPsec. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create a Site-to-Site VPN connection over the internet from the data center router to a virtual private gateway that is attached to the VPC.
options.why: The VPN is quick to create, but [performance over the internet is best effort](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-vs-vpn-internet-vpn-best-effort-low-cost-widely-available), so it does not give consistent performance.
options.misconception: a VPN over the internet gives consistent network performance

options.text: Order a new AWS Direct Connect dedicated connection, and create a Site-to-Site VPN connection over it from the data center router to the VPC.
options.why: Direct Connect gives [more consistent performance than the internet can provide](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-decision-guide-more-consistent-performance-than-internet), and a VPN over it gives [an IPsec-encrypted private connection](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-plus-site-to-site-vpn-ipsec-encrypted-private-connection).

options.text: Launch a software VPN appliance on an Amazon EC2 instance in the VPC, and connect it to the data center router with IPsec over the internet.
options.why: The appliance still sends IPsec across the internet, where [performance over the internet is best effort](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-vs-vpn-internet-vpn-best-effort-low-cost-widely-available), and the team also patches it.
options.misconception: a VPN appliance that the company runs itself removes the variability of the internet path

options.text: Order a new AWS Direct Connect dedicated connection, and launch a software VPN appliance on an Amazon EC2 instance that ends IPsec over the connection.
options.why: It works, but [you must manage the software appliance](../facts/site-to-site-vpn.md#site-to-site-vpn-software-vpn-ec2-you-manage-appliance-single-point-of-failure); a Site-to-Site VPN over the same connection encrypts without an instance to run.

items.explanation: The deciding phrase is consistent network performance for large, steady transfers. Direct Connect fits it, but it [does not encrypt your traffic](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-not-encrypted-by-default-use-service-encryption) by default. To encrypt, you [establish a VPN over Direct Connect](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-encrypt-private-connection-vpn-over-dx-or-macsec), which needs no instance to run.
items.takeaway: Consistent performance points to Direct Connect, and a Site-to-Site VPN over it adds IPsec encryption.
items.twin: If the stem said "The connection must be ready as soon as possible, within one week, and the traffic is low" instead: a Site-to-Site VPN over the internet, because it [can be configured in minutes](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-faq-vpn-ipsec-over-internet-quick-low-bandwidth).
items.say: For steady, large transfers I'd use Direct Connect and run a Site-to-Site VPN over it for encryption.

solvers.stem_only: Order an AWS Direct Connect dedicated connection for consistent performance and run an AWS Site-to-Site VPN (IPsec) over it from the data center router for encryption.

items.stem: A company sends traffic from its data center to a VPC over a private line: an AWS Direct Connect connection with a private virtual interface. A new security rule says that all traffic on this connection must be encrypted in transit. The connection is a 10 Gbps dedicated connection, the router and location support MACsec, and the encryption must not reduce the MTU. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: the router and location support MACsec

options.text: Turn on MACsec for the Direct Connect connection, and configure the matching MACsec keys on the company router at the Direct Connect location.
options.why: MACsec runs on [10 Gbps, 100 Gbps, and 400 Gbps dedicated AWS Direct Connect connections](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-macsec-supported-dedicated-10-100-400-gbps), and [MACsec does not have the same MTU](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-vpn-over-dx-adds-encryption-reduces-mtu) considerations that a VPN has.

options.text: Create a Site-to-Site VPN connection that runs IPsec over the Direct Connect connection, and route the VPC traffic through the VPN tunnels.
options.why: A VPN over Direct Connect adds encryption, but [it reduces the MTU size](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-vpn-over-dx-adds-encryption-reduces-mtu), so it breaks the MTU requirement.
options.misconception: a VPN over Direct Connect keeps the full MTU of the link

options.text: Keep the current design, because traffic on a Direct Connect connection stays off the internet and is encrypted on the private line.
options.why: Direct Connect [does not encrypt your traffic](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-not-encrypted-by-default-use-service-encryption) in transit by default, so the private line alone breaks the new security rule.

options.text: Turn on TLS encryption in every application that sends data between the data center and the VPC, and keep the virtual interface unchanged.
options.why: It works, because you can [use the transit encryption options for that service](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-not-encrypted-by-default-use-service-encryption), but changing every application is more work than MACsec on one link.

items.explanation: The deciding phrases are the 10 Gbps dedicated connection and the MTU. MACsec is supported on [10 Gbps, 100 Gbps, and 400 Gbps dedicated AWS Direct Connect connections](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-macsec-supported-dedicated-10-100-400-gbps), and [you will need a MACsec-capable device](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-faq-macsec-needs-capable-device), which the company router is. A VPN would also encrypt, but [it reduces the MTU size](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-vpn-over-dx-adds-encryption-reduces-mtu).
items.takeaway: When the router and the location support MACsec, MACsec encrypts the link without the MTU cost of an IPsec VPN.
items.twin: If the stem said "The connection is a 1 Gbps hosted connection from a Direct Connect Partner" instead: an IPsec VPN over Direct Connect, because MACsec does not run on [any hosted connections](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-macsec-not-on-1gbps-or-hosted).
items.say: On a 10 gig dedicated connection with a MACsec router, I'd turn on MACsec, because it keeps the MTU.

solvers.stem_only: Turn on MACsec on the 10 Gbps dedicated connection and configure the matching keys (CKN/CAK) on the router; layer-2 encryption without the IPsec MTU and throughput penalty.
